Research task, read-only, no repo changes. Investigate what the old Sun Fortress project website contained, to decide what's worth migrating into a new README for the github.com/palimondo/fortress revival (the repo already has Sun's SVN-era README.txt — 644 lines of checkout instructions and a subdirectory tour — so only content NOT in that file is interesting).

The site was projectfortress.sun.com (2006–2010), later java.net/projects/projectfortress (2010–2012/13, after Oracle moved it), possibly also research.sun.com/projects/plrg pages. All are dead; use the Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) via WebFetch/WebSearch. HTTPS goes through a proxy; if a fetch fails oddly just try another snapshot/URL form.

What to look for:
1. The project front-page pitch: how Sun described Fortress (taglines, elevator pitch) — quotable material for a README history section.
2. Lists of publications/papers with titles (especially anything beyond: the Fortress language spec, the Growing a Language talk, OOPSLA/PLDI papers on components/traits/multiple dispatch/implicit parallelism, the HPCS/DARPA context).
3. Community/ecosystem facts: mailing lists, blog posts of note, the wiki, release timeline (Fortress 1.0 spec March 2008; the 2012 "wind-down" announcement by Guy Steele — find the exact wording/date of that announcement if archived, it's historically important).
4. Anything else a revival README should link or record (e.g., the wind-down FAQ, interpreter release notes, "Project Fortress at Oracle Labs" pages).

Do NOT fetch or reproduce anything at length; short quotes with archive.org URLs are what I need. Report back compactly: per finding — what it is, best archive.org URL, and a 1-2 line summary or key quote. List dead ends too (what you tried that isn't archived). Your final message is data for me, not for the user.

Index of primary sources on the design and history of Fortress, maintained as
part of the revival effort. **Links and metadata only** — the documents
themselves are copyrighted (Oracle's notice permits personal/classroom copies
but not redistribution), so PDFs live in `decks/`, which is gitignored and
local-only: drop the files in manually each session; they are never committed.
`extracts/` holds committed working notes on the sources — our own summaries
and commentary with brief attributed quotations, never document reproductions.

## Talks and decks

- **JuliaCon 2016 keynote — "Fortress Features and Lessons Learned"**

 I am not surprised... 
 It's not that easy to target an arbitrary virtual machine. For instance, almost all compilers I know target an abstract assembly in which the basic allocation unit is a cell, which may hold either a pointer or an integer of register size, sometimes another small value. Moreover, a number of target assembly languages then continue to allow for pointer arithmetic in order to implement fast branching. AFAIK, both are impossible in the Java VM, at least, not without a performance hit. 
 Then there is RTTI which may not map into the Java manner of keeping track of types, forcing one to generate another layer of RTTI on top of Java. 
 Then there is the fact that it is a mostly functional language; meaning it will allocate an enormous amount runtime, which might be slow in Java. Plus that I don't know how efficiently Java reduces closures; which may be another runtime penalty. 
 Lastly, Fortress sits in the same solution space as Haskell and ML. Why target a VM inefficiently when there are other languages who already fill the same niche which enjoy a larger audience? 
 For a sufficiently complex language, there are usually more reasons not to target a Java VM, or .NET for that matter. Targeting a Java VM is mostly for untyped scripting languages, or 'cheap' Java knock-offs. (Or those languages which can get away with an AST reducer.)

There are people out there who might use it for free, but almost no one will pay for it. And, even if they did, there aren't enough people willing to pay to make a strong business case. 
 The starting market for developer tools in the HPC space is developers who work on scientific or HPC projects. Across the world, that on the order of 1k-10k developers total, across all scientific domains. Note that this excludes technical end users such as those that may use Matlab or IDL, though that market isn't much larger.

"Fortress, a new language designed specifically for high-performance computing (HPC), has been released on SunSource under the BSD language."

The article describes Fortress as "intended as a modern day replacement for Fortran." Key technical features highlighted include support for "mathematical notation and static checking of physical units and dimensions," with "many of the core language constructs are parallel by default."

- Main project site: fortress.sunsource.net

The work was created as part of Sun's involvement in the DARPA HPCS program. Though Sun was subsequently eliminated from that program, Guy Steele continued development through Sun's Programming Language Research Group.

"The preliminary interpreter is based on the JVM," though the article notes indicators suggesting Fortress "may eventually have its own virtual machine" due to different memory models and planned software transactional memory support.
